note: Vol. I No. 13, and the most consequential issue of the month: on page 2 column 6 the Chicago river, swollen by Friday's rain, cuts its own channel over the bar at the mouth of the harbour then building, seven to eight feet deep. The town is also on page 3 columns 2, 3 and 6 and page 4 column 2. A livery stable opens at the Point, Elston fits up a smoke house, a fire-eater performs in Graves's tavern, and the county clerk's office moves one door west of Col. Owen's house.

claims.notes:
THE RIVER CUT ITS OWN HARBOUR MOUTH, IN ONE NIGHT, AND THE PAPER MEASURED IT. This is the most consequential dated reading in the month. Rain on Friday 14 February 1834 swelled the Chicago river; on the Saturday the flood, driving the winter's ice ahead of it, forced a passage OVER THE BAR at the mouth of the harbour then under construction, and by Saturday evening a channel stood open SEVEN TO EIGHT FEET DEEP. The width figure is lost at the column edge and is left unsupplied. Nearly all the water of the river was afterwards running to the lake through the new cut rather than through the old channel, and the paper credits the pier with directing it.

WHAT IT FIXES FOR A RECONSTRUCTION STANDING IN JULY 1835. The three harbour readings this corpus now holds are a sequence with dates on it: January 1834, the engineer's report — almost nothing built, materials unobtainable, the first proposals rejected as exorbitant. 4 February 1834, Lieut. J. Allen appointed superintendent. 15 February 1834, THE BAR IS BREACHED and the river's mouth moves to where the works wanted it, saving what the editor reckons would have been several hundred hands' work. By August 1834 the North Pier is being run out across the sand-bar by about a hundred hands. So the straight cut to the lake that the scene date takes for granted begins in a February flood, and the men on the bar that day were helping the water rather than digging.

The column is interleaved with the prairie-timber essay beside it line for line; `lines_of_claim` names only the lines the harbour paragraph can be followed through, and single stray words inside the range are excluded.

claims.notes: THE COOK COUNTY MEETING OF 15 FEBRUARY, ADJOURNED — the meeting the two previous issues called to the Eagle Hotel, with Richard J. Hamilton in the chair and P. F. W. Peck as secretary. Hamilton is the clerk of the circuit court whose name attests the stray-cattle notices in every issue of the month; Peck keeps the store at La Salle and South Water and reports the paper's prices. Only the closing lines of the proceedings survive the column edge, so the resolutions themselves are not claimed; what is claimed is that the meeting happened, on the day it was called for, and who ran it.

First, the October 1834 read had to refuse a Plainfield letter list as not Chicago's, and this is where that office comes from — it is nine months old at that point. Second, it is a measure of the county filling in around the town in the year and a half before the scene date. The place name is set 'Walker's C[…]' here and is Walker's GROVE in the stage-coach advertisement two pages on in the same issue; the transcription's 'Paink' is read as Plainfield on the strength of the later lists.

claims.notes: A FIRE-EATER IN THE TAVERN, AT EARLY CANDLE LIGHT. This is the best piece of interior evidence the month yields, and it is about a building this project has to imagine: Dexter Graves's house has a room large enough to seat an audience with SEATS PRESERVED FOR LADIES, it has a BAR that sells the tickets, and it is lit well enough to perform in after dark in February. The performance is repeated on the Wednesday evening of the following week (1834-02-25, claim c003), so the room was worth hiring twice.\n\nGRAVES'S HOUSE IS THE MONTH'S BUSIEST ANCHOR: the tin and stove maker J. K. Botsford advertises 'next door to Graves' Tavern' and the smith Matthias Mason 'back on Main-street, nearly opposite Graves' Tavern'. Three separate businesses and a public entertainment place themselves against it inside three weeks, which makes it the one building on the north side of the town's business row that this corpus can treat as a fixed point — and Botsford's other advertisement gives that point a corner. See 1834-02-25 claim c005.

claims.notes: A LIVERY STABLE OPENS AT THE POINT, in February 1834, and it is a NEW building's worth of use for a place this project already models. 'The Point' is Wolf Point, the fork where the two branches meet, and it is the only structure this corpus places there. What the advertisement gives beyond the site is the trade: saddle horses and SINGLE HORSE CARRIAGES to hire day or night, cash only, and horses kept by the day or week for people who came into town and needed them stabled. That is a yard with stalls and standing room, not a shed — and it stands where every road into the town converged before the Dearborn street bridge existed. The placement is `relative` on the Point rather than `corner`, because the Point is a landform and not a street junction: this claim names the neighbourhood and cannot name the lot.

claims.notes: A NEW BUILDING, NAMED, DATED AND FUNCTIONAL: Daniel Elston & Co. have FITTED UP A SMOKE HOUSE and are ready to begin curing on 15 February 1834. This is the second working structure the month adds to the town after the livery stable at the Point, and it is the more suggestive of the two, because a smoke house is a small windowless outbuilding with a fire in it standing near — but deliberately not against — whatever else its owner has. Elston already runs the Chicago Soap and Candle Manufactory, a works that renders tallow and buys house ashes off the town; hams, flitches of bacon and mess pork are the same trade's other half. NO ADDRESS is given for either the works or the smoke house in any printing this corpus holds, so nothing is placed by this claim — but a reconstruction that wants an industrial corner of the town now has two named processes to put in it.

claims.notes: HOW YOU GOT TO CHICAGO OVERLAND IN FEBRUARY 1834, in the coach proprietors' own numbers. From Ottawa by Holderman's Grove, Walker's Grove and Laughton's: SIXTY MILES, once a week, three and a half days, five dollars. The Galena coach leaves Chicago EVERY THURSDAY — the same morning the eastern, western and northern mails go out under the postmaster's timetable in the previous issue, which is not a coincidence but the same connection seen from both ends. St. Louis is six days off, travelling by daylight only.\n\nWHAT IT IS WORTH TO A RECONSTRUCTION: it prices the town's isolation. A place that is three and a half days from Ottawa by four-horse post coach and six days from St. Louis is a place whose building materials come by water when the lake opens and not otherwise, which is exactly what the winter advertising columns show — everything for sale in February was landed before the ice. It also names Laughton's as a stage stop, and Laughton's tavern on the Des Plaines is a known fixed point on the road west.

claims.notes: A CIVIC OFFICE PLACED AGAINST A PRIVATE HOUSE, which is how this town describes itself. The clerk of the circuit and county courts — Richard J. Hamilton, whose signature attests the estray notices in every issue — moves his office to THE BUILDING ONE DOOR WEST OF THE HOUSE OF COL. OWEN. Col. Owen is Thomas J. V. Owen, the Indian agent, and his house is one of the few dwellings in the town a reconstruction has any independent record of. The 4 February printing of this same notice lost the destination entirely; this one carries it whole, and the 25 February one repeats it. Recorded as a business with a `relative` placement because that is the vocabulary the gazetteer has for a premises counted off a neighbour, and the county clerk's office was a premises: a room the public came to.

claims.notes: CHICAGO'S TRADE ROUTES, WRITTEN OUT AS SIX NAMES. Kinzie's references are his correspondents, and they map the town's commercial reach in February 1834: New York and Buffalo down the lakes, Detroit across it, Green Bay and Prairie du Chien north and west into the fur country, Galena for the lead. Joseph Rolette at Prairie du Chien is an American Fur Company man; so, by descent, is Kinzie. What this is worth to a reconstruction is the mix on the wharves — a warehouse here was handling eastern dry goods inbound and northwestern peltry and Galena lead outbound, and the two do not look alike. He still gives no address.

claims.notes:
THE SIXTH PRINTING OF THE FIRST HALF, AND IT MINTS NOBODY — but it is the printing that lets several of the minted names be read at all. The list is minted from 1834-02-04 for A-H and 1834-02-11 for H-W, and every other printing is a reprint under the one-list-one-cohort rule set out in the 4 February claim. This column is nonetheless a better witness than most: it is the only one that carries CONSTANT ABBOTT, WM. G. AUSTIN, MYRON K. BROWNSON and TIMOTHY BURNETT, four names that stand in no other February printing and in none of the January ones, and it is where 'Aarrist Bradford' is confirmed as HARRIET and 'Grastus Bowen' can be checked.

WHY THEY ARE NOT MINTED ANYWAY. Because the alternative is the defect T-0299 records — one list minting its people two and three times over as the OCR spells them differently in each printing — and a rule that admits an exception for four names admits it for forty. The four are named here, in a claim that quotes them, so the next pass can mint them deliberately if the project decides the rule should be per-name rather than per-half. That is a decision about the corpus and not a reading of this issue.

The column is interleaved with two poems line for line; `lines_of_claim` names the lines the list can be followed through.
